en: Now, the *Śrīvātūlanāthasūtrāṇi*, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Anantaśaktipāda: 1ab: The state of the Void beyond the Void, which is free from modification and arises through the power of the friction of union, is the essence of imperishable consciousness.

I bow to that which shines everywhere through the vision of the sky-farer (*khecarī*), the supreme audacious [reality] accessible only from the mouth of the Guru. May that unborn one, whose nature is the unsurpassed sky of consciousness, be victorious— he who, by the mode of transcending all, is here free from mental constructs, beyond sequence and non-sequence.
I bow to that which arises from the ocean of the heart of the illustrious Vātūlanātha, which is utterly devoid of the worshiped, the worshiper, and the act of worship; by means of which,
even while always situated in the midst of all mental fluctuations in this world, [one remains established].
4cd: Pervading the great void, I abide here without any succession.
5ab: That which is unprecedented, without immersion, untouched, and without abode— 5cd:
I bow to that unsurpassed state, which is the friction of consciousness, conceptualization, and volition.
6ab: An excellent commentary on the Sūtras born from the mouth of the Yoginī is being composed by someone. 6cd: It is thoroughly augmented by the Supreme Reality;
indeed, here [is presented] that which transcends all philosophical systems—from the six Darśanas and the four Āmnāyas up to the Melāpas—though it is ineffable.

Having spoken of the lineage of the feet of Ucchuṣma, the Mistress of the Seat (pīṭheśvarī) of the illustrious Vātūlanātha, they then point out— by means of aphorisms— that certain supreme reality which is devoid of the stain of worldly existence and liberation, including sequence and non-sequence, existence and non-existence, truth and untruth, difference and non-difference, and the conceptual and the non-conceptual; this reality is perceived through the vision of the direct realization of the thirteen discourses augmented by the supreme secret.
Regarding this first sūtra: "The attainment of its own nature occurs through the Mahāsāhasrī commentary. (VaSu 1)

For someone who has been struck by an exceedingly intense, even more intense, and unimpeded descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and who is thus immersed in their own true nature, there occurs— spontaneously, at some time and in some place, through the "mode of great daring" (*mahāsāhasavṛtti*)— an expansion of the manifestation of another Name that is more voracious and dense than the Great [Name]. Through this, by the shattering of the entire mass of cognitions consisting of both conceptual and non-conceptual forms, one reaches the culmination of absorption into the Great Void (*mahāśūnyatā*) which is free from all veils.

The secret meaning is this: "the attainment of one's own true nature" (*svarūpalābha*) occurs as the realization of a consciousness that is uncreated, without room for [duality], unsurpassed, waveless, limitless, homeless, and untouched; for it transcends all conceptual constructions.
Furthermore, the entry into the practice of "great audacity" (*mahāsāhasavṛtti*) is to be understood through the sequence that will be explained below.

Having first established the tradition of the discourse on the great audacity (*mahāsāhasa*) consisting of the direct realization of the attainment of the nature of the homeless state through the method of instantaneous transcendence of all things,
they now describe therein the great aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) of all mental fluctuations at a single time;
for by attaining that, one is permeated with it.

The simultaneous arising and functioning of the mental states (*vṛtti*)— which take the form of rays such as sight and so forth, as well as the manifestation of passion, aversion, and the like— is "simultaneous" (*yugapat*), meaning at the same time,

by way of a non-sequential progression that transcends the order of succession. It is "suffused by the attainment of that" (*tallābhācchuritā*), meaning by that [attainment] which is reached through the process of immersion into the previously described state of great audacity (*mahāsāhasa*).

"Active state" (*pravṛtti*)— meaning a state that exists with excellence, a continuous abiding in absorption with that [Reality] through perpetual non-falling— is "smeared," touched, and brought to its own true nature by that which has transcended the conceptualization of time and non-time through the attainment of its own essential form, whose body is the full swallowing [of all things], and which is utterly free from effort. By this turn of expression, immediately after all [limited] functions, [the soul] is established in the abode of the Great Void, which is the very nature of the Light and transcends everything.
The meaning is that "staying" (sthiti) refers to remaining constantly on the very plane of emergence through identification with That, by means of the dissolution of mutual differentiation.
Having thus stated the instruction on simultaneous narration through this method of expression, they now describe the narrative of the book (*pustaka-kathā*):
"By the opening of both flaps, there is entry into the Great Void;

at the time of the grace of the venerable Niṣkriyānandanātha, that very attainment in the supreme state which was taught by the venerable Siddhapāda of Gandhamādana through the display of the uncreated book is here described in detail."

The upward band (*ūrdhvapaṭṭaka*) is the emergence of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of the radiance of the seven crests arising through the sequence of the seven apertures; it is the emergence of the full functional state.

The downward band (*adhaḥpaṭṭaka*), which is of the nature of the downward breath (*apāna*), extends from the channel of the two apertures and cavities; it is encircled by the powers of the five senses, bound by the qualities of the five hoods, and situated below.
By "unfastening both bands," one uncovers its two coils—which consist of the waking and dreaming states—and removes the binding of the knots.

That which abides in the center, having split apart the pair of prāṇa and apāna, is the nature of great emptiness in the form of prāṇa; it is abandoned by the state of conceptualizing kula and akula, is inexpressible, free from the great obscuration and the faultless duality of the known and the knower, transcends color, non-color, and absence of color, and— by way of relinquishing the manifestation of touch and non-touch—
is designated by such names as "supreme space" and so forth.
It is explained as follows:

therein, "entry" (*praveśa*) means the state of being established in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) through immersion in that [reality]; the meaning is that this very state manifests as what is called the "Great Instruction" (*mahopadeśa*).

Thus, according to the perspective taught in the Mahānaya, having explained that which is inexpressible— because it transcends the manifold elaborations of all scriptures— a certain Great Instruction (*mahopadeśa*) that is directly realized; which,

by eliminating the duality of existence and non-existence in the form of the two tablets, is free from immersion in the waveless supreme sky, and is the realization of the Great Void (*mahāśūnyatā*) as it has been indicated.

Now, following the conclusion regarding the pairs, the fruit of isolation (*kaivalya*)—which consists of being absorbed in that [Reality]—is described: "Through the swallowing of the pairs, consciousness comes to rest in the state of having no further space [for duality]. (VaSu 4)
Within each of the five great elements, beginning with earth, there is an established arrangement of a "pair" (*yugma*) arising through the mode of functioning as the grasped and the grasper.

In that regard, because smell is predominant, the *dharātattva* (earth-principle) possesses a twofold nature in the form of the anus and the nose; and because taste is predominant, the *aptattva* (water-principle) possesses a twofold nature in the form of the generative organ and the tongue.
Because the fire element (*tejastattva*) has form (*rūpa*) as its primary quality, it possesses a twofold nature through the distinction of feet and eyes.
Because the air element (*vāyutattva*) has touch (*sparśa*) as its primary quality, its movement is twofold by virtue of its essential nature as skin and hands.
Because the space element (*ākāśatattva*) has sound (*śabda*) as its primary quality, it exists in many ways precisely through its twofold modality as speech and hearing.
Alternatively, earth and water exist in the form of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*),
while fire and air exist as the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
This ether (*ākāśa*), situated between this pair, exists as a state of perfect porosity, arising within all the channels and divided in many ways.

Alternatively, it may be that the four elements from earth up to air are of the nature of the object of experience (*bhogya*), while space is of the nature of the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). Even within the object of experience, the experiencer always abides; likewise, even within the experiencer, there is the object of experience.
It shines eternally.

The intended meaning is that, according to the reasoning thus stated, each of the five great elements, beginning with earth, incessantly radiates forth through a pair—that is, by means of a twofold manifestation.
Alternatively, it shines individually as manifest and unmanifest, as external and internal, or as tranquil and excited.

From the "devouring" (*grāsāt*), that is, from the withdrawal of this pair established in the five locations, there arises the "culmination of spaceless consciousness" (*niravakāśasaṃvinniṣṭhā*). This means the firm establishment (*saṃsthiti*) of that very consciousness which is spaceless, by virtue of its being perfectly non-erroneous. Because it is spaceless consciousness, no room is found even for the emergences of conceptual consciousness (*savikalpasaṃvidunmeṣaiḥ*).
Nor is entry attained by way of the nature of non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-saṃvit*).
Thus, because it is immeasurable and because its nature is the unsurpassed, supreme non-duality, this is called "consciousness without scope" (*niravakāśa-saṃvit*).
The meaning is that its culmination occurs for some as a constant state, according to the vision shown by the excellent Guru.

Thus, by means of the devouring of Kulakaula, which consists of these two, there arises identity with that which is free from limiting conditions, formless, and devoid of specific nature; this is the meaning. //4//

Having explained the abiding in the supreme reality through the dissolution of duality by means of this progression of the discussion on the Couple, thereupon the direct realization of the discourse on union (*saṃghaṭṭa*) is described:
"From the union of the Siddhas and Yoginīs, the arising of the Great Assembly (*mahāmelāpa*) occurs. (VaSu 5)
The *siddhas* and the *yoginīs* are the *siddhayoginīs*, who are the forms of the sovereign goddesses of the sense objects and the faculties.

Their *saṃghaṭṭa*—their union, the mutual embrace through the sequence of mutual incitement—is the fusion of both the grasped and the grasper. Through that embrace, there is always the "arising of the Great Conjunction" (*mahāmelāpa*), because of the dissolution of duality consisting of "I-ness" and "this-ness" within the Great Conjunction.

The meaning is that there occurs a constant arising, a full-blown manifestation, within the unsurpassed sky of consciousness which consists of the great state of aesthetic equilibrium (*mahāsāmarasya*) and is directly perceptible everywhere.

By means of the activity of not manifesting the duality of the object and the subject, it is stated that the immersion into supreme non-duality (*paramādvayasamāveśa*) is established everywhere. //5//
Having stated that the arising of the Great Union (*mahāmelāpa*) occurs through the constant shedding of both [subject and object],
they thereafter indicate the attainment of the unsurpassed state by transcending the three coverings (*kañcuka*):
"Through the abandonment of the three coverings, there is abiding in the ineffable state (*nirākhya-pada*)."
Of the triple casing (trikañcuka), which is divided into the categories of the real (bhāvika), the elemental (bhautika), and the void (śūnya):
therein, the "real" consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra) beginning with sound and ending with ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra);
the "elemental" consists of the forms of earth and the other gross elements.
It is either empty, called "inactive," and having the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
or else it is the external, objective form of the jar which is real, while the internal,
elemental form consists of the sense organs and has the nature of the subject that grasps.
That which is empty is the intermediate space between those two;
alternatively, the creation of the dream state is called the phenomenal (bhāvika),
while the manifestation of the waking state is described as the material (bhautika).
The void state of deep sleep is designated as *saṃhāra* (reabsorption).

For one who is thus situated within the triple sheath (*trikañcuka*), "by means of abandonment"—that is, through renunciation (*sannyāsa*)—there occurs "abiding in the state beyond designation" (*nirākhyapadāvasthiti*). That which has departed from all names and designations is "the nameless" (*nirākhya*); it is the ineffable, supreme abode that transcends speech, the Absolute (*anuttara*).

The connection is that in that supreme space, which transcends all abodes and is without a dwelling place, there is a state of constant abiding characterized by a persistence in one's own nature from which one is never fallen away. //6//
Having thus described the attainment of the fourth state (*turyapada*) by transcending the three sheaths (*kañcuka*),
they now demonstrate that within all manifestations of speech, when they are free from obscuration, there always shines forth only the unfolding of the power of the primordial sound (*svarabhūti*).
Regarding the manifestation of the emergence and cessation of the fourfold speech (*vākcatuṣṭaya*), the *svara* (vowel/tonal resonance) expands at the beginning;
first, therefore, the fourfold speech is determined.

Its nature is the expansion of the first vibration (*spanda*), which consists of a slight movement surging forth within the supreme ether that is unobstructed, without interval, unsurpassed, and waveless.

That [Speech] which, through the state of non-dual great aesthetic equilibrium (*mahāsāmarasya*), holds the arrangement of phonemes within itself according to the analogy of the fluid within a peacock’s egg, is celebrated as *Parā*.

That very same [Speech], having attained the nature of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) and possessing an indivisible character, holds the emergence of all phonemes within itself like the seed-vessel of a banyan tree; being of the nature of the seer, it is designated as *Paśyantī*.

And that same [Speech], having taken possession of the ground of the intellect (*buddhi*) whose essence consists of the determination of the multitude of conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations, holds the mass of phonemes within itself according to the analogy of the seed-pod of a *śimbikā* fruit; she is called *Madhyamā*.

That very [power], when struck by the sequence of places and articulators such as the heart, throat, and palate, manifests differentiated forms like verses composed of a wealth of phonemes; and by bringing about the manifestation of the entire universe, including form and so forth, it is called *vaikharī*.
Thus, from that which has no [other] space...
From the state of pure consciousness (*saṃvit*), the fourfold speech unfolds incessantly due to its unceasing nature.
Thus, the emergence and the cessation of this fourfold speech, which is of such a nature, are themselves emergence and cessation— that is, emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
The manifestation (*prathā*) of those two [the manifest and the unmanifest] always shines forth and vibrates incessantly;

within them, "sound" (*svara*), whose nature is the expansion and blossoming of the Great Sound that transcends both the unstruck (*anāhata*) and the struck (*hata*), "manifests"— meaning it proceeds by way of effortless activity, constantly illuminating the very arising of the supreme ether (*paraviyat*) which transcends conceptual and non-conceptual consciousness.

Thus, from within the mass of phonemes that arise as the manifestation of various distinct forms of light, each individual phoneme shines forth by its own very nature—without abandoning its essential form and through the uninterrupted operation of the sequence of the fourfold speech—according to the method taught by the Teacher;
this is what is meant. //7//

Having thus established that the unobscured emergence of the vowels (*svarodaya*) vibrates everywhere and at all times through the sequence of the arising of the fourfold speech, [the author now states:
when there is the enjoyment of the three *rasas*, the supreme abode alone shines forth as unsurpassed.
Thus it is said:
through the tasting of the three flavors, the supreme Brahman—free from bonds and surging forth without desire—is realized.
The three nectars (*rasatraya*) are briefly and slightly revealed through the perspective taught by the mouth of the Guru.

When there is the full enjoyment of the threefold natural nectar (*akṛtrima-rasatritaya*) celebrated as being supported by the cloud-breast of the *mūlādhāra*, that which has "surged forth without desire" (*anicchocchalitam*)—

meaning it has blossomed through freedom from longing— and which is "freed from bonds" (*vigatabandham*), meaning it is devoid of the obstruction of saṃsāra consisting of the manifestation of duality.

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman alone— which transcends both the tranquil and the manifold aspects of the nature of Brahman, and whose essence is an unsurpassed, most excellent awareness (*āmarśa*) and consciousness— continually unfolds through a state that never sets.
This very point is expressed according to the secret tradition (*rahasyakrama*).

The *mūlādhāra* (root-support), however, is the great resonance (*mahānāda*) of the first flash of intuition (*pratibhā*), whose nature is emission (*sṛṣṭi*); it is so called because it serves as the foundational wall for the primary locus of the categories of consciousness, which consist of both difference and non-difference. The *payodhara* (cloud-bearer/mountain), however, is the very nature of all-encompassing consciousness, which sustains—that is, supports the growth and stability of—that same [emission]; it is of the nature of maintenance (*sthiti*), like the upward expansion of the breath (*unmeṣa*), because it manifests all objects. As for the *ādhāra* (support):
Because it withdraws all objects of existence, whether insentient or sentient, *saṃhāra* (withdrawal) is by nature the consciousness of reversion (*pratyāvṛtti*).

Having savored this form of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which is the essence of the three [stages] shaken off and the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) consisting of the wonder of various experiences, and having contemplated it through entry into the uncreated seal of emptiness within one's own self, the nature of the Fourth (*turya*)—known as the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra*)—shines forth incessantly as supreme non-duality; such is the secret meaning. //8//
Having thus established the tradition of the discourse on the three *rasas* through an approach that leaves no room for alternative views,
the direct realization of the narrative of the four goddesses is now revealed:
"Through the manifestation of the four goddesses, there is always the state of abiding in one's own rest."
The "four goddesses" are known as hunger, thirst, envy, and pride.
Among them, because it is intent upon devouring everything, hunger itself is the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra*).
Because it dries up everything, thirst itself is the Withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Envy is that which brings about the manifestation of duality; it is a state bound by the grasping of subject and object, and its nature is stability.
And mentation is creation, whose nature is the surging of conceptualization and discursive thought.
Through the "surging" (*ullāsena*)—that is, through the unfolding and the proceeding of the flow of voracious consciousness—of this fourfold group of goddesses whose form is thus constituted.

The meaning of “*sadaiva*” (always) is that at all times, through each of the fourfold self-natures, there is an abiding in one’s own essential nature— consisting of the manifestation of effort, its relishing, and its full assimilation— which transcends the fifth state and culminates in an unrestricted consciousness.
Having thus revealed the sequence of the discourse on the four goddesses by means of this aphorism, [the text continues].
Now the secret of the wheel of the twelve currents is described:
"By the arising of the twelve currents, there is the blossoming of the great rays. (VaSu)
The five sense organs, beginning with the ear, are conjoined with the mind (*manas*);
likewise, the five organs of action, beginning with speech, are conjoined with the intellect (*buddhi*).
This aggregate of both is the "twelvefold flow" (*dvādaśavāha*).
Its radiance (*ullāsa*) is a voracious flow of consciousness by means of some causeless, utterly unconditioned state of being—the activity of supreme freedom that is unsurpassed and waveless.

Through this, there occurs the "expansion" (*vikāsa*) of the "great rays" (*mahāmarīcīnām*)—that is, the rays of great consciousness whose nature consists in resting upon the complete grasping, savoring, manifestation, and exertion of effort within each [moment] through the process of removal of veils; it is a nature that is eternally blossoming due to the dissolving away of the manifestation of limited and unlimited consciousness and unconsciousness.
The meaning of the Great Saying (mahāvākya) is that the Great Awakening, by virtue of its perpetual indestructibility, abides everywhere, in every way, and at all times.
Thus, having revealed that which is established by non-action as the perpetual immersion in the state free from obscuration through the vision of the arising of the twelve flows,
they now describe the tradition of the fivefold conduct (*caryāpañcaka*):
"In the arising of the fivefold conduct, there is immersion free of waves."
The *Caryāpañcaka*, however, has as its essential nature the Anāśrita, Avadhūta, Unmatta, Sarvabhakṣya, and Mahāvyāpaka.
Its arising (*udaya*) is the expansion and effulgence of the innate nature, which emerges from within the collection of both fixed and unfixed powers.

When that occurs, the meaning is that the "waveless immersion" (*nistaraṅga-samāveśa*)—the dharma of the unsurpassed immersion characterized by an immersion devoid of all waves consisting of the arising of the Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava [states]—manifests itself.
I shall now set forth and examine the sequence of the five modes of conduct (*caryā*).

Among these, *Anāśritā* is so called because, being without support, she takes the form of the supreme space; she has arisen for the purpose of withdrawing her own objects of perception by entering the region of the auditory cavity. *Avadhūtā*, on the other hand, is so called because, through her lack of fixedness, she has opened wide to appropriate what is to be withdrawn by herself, via the path of the power of vision that dwells everywhere.
And she is "mad" (*unmattā*), renowned for grasping her own objects through her independence, without intending to distinguish between what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped.

She is "all-devouring" (*sarvabhakṣyā*), characterized by swallowing all morsels of the refinement of the edible and inedible, and arisen for the purpose of devouring those things that are to be withdrawn by herself.
And she is "all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpikā*).
Through the process of the functioning of the skin, [consciousness] has emerged because it pervades everything and because it grasps all tactile sensations;
such is the arising of the fivefold conduct (*caryā*).

Having examined the sequence of the practice of the eternally perfected ones (*siddha*), Vasugupta now examines the discourse on the cessation of merit and demerit by relying upon the illumination of supreme knowledge that is free from abode:
"Through immersion into Great Awakening (*mahābodha*), there is a connection with merit and demerit. (Note: This implies their transcendence.)

“Great Awakening” (*mahābodha*) is that which is free from the turbidity of conceptualization and mental construction regarding the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge; it consists of the manifestation of the supreme light, the abode of both cessation and non-cessation, and has the nature of the highest gnosis. Because it transcends both sequence and non-sequence, it is directly realized by the Great Gurus.

Its “immersion” (*samāveśa*) is the constant flashing forth in that very form through a state of non-falling away—by means of the process of non-action, in its natural state of being, and by way of relinquishing all acceptance and rejection.

Therefore, through "immersion in Great Awakening (*mahābodhasamāveśa*)," there is for the heroic hero of the last birth— someone who, while still living, is perpetually satisfied by chewing on the flavor of uncreated experience at all times— an "absence of connection," a lack of attachment and non-union with both merit and demerit, that is, with the two types of karma characterized as auspicious and inauspicious which have the nature of bestowing their own respective fruits. This is the Great Liberation, transcending both bondage and liberation, occurring right here on the plane of phenomenal existence.
The meaning is that it stands as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Having explained the sequence of discourse regarding the setting aside of merit and sin preceded by the attainment of one's own true nature, Vasu now introduces the discourse on the silence established in its own essence:
"Through the power of the discourse on non-discourse, by attaining the seal of great wonder, there is the state of the Sky-Sound (*khasvara*)."

"The power of the discourse on the inexpressible" (*akathanakathābala*) is here briefly discussed according to the sequence of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) taught from the mouth of the Guru. Regarding this letter *A*:

because it has transcended the struck (*hata*) [sound] of the unstruck (*anāhata*), its manifestation in four ways constitutes the "inexpressible" (*akathana*), which is the arrangement of the discussion based on the oral lineage (*vaktrāmnāya*).

In this regard, the *hata* (struck) sound is first described: it is that which, through the arrangement of the locations (*sthāna*) and articulators (*karaṇa*) such as the heart, throat, and palate, manifests various objects from the letter *a* to the letter *ha*. The *anāhata* (unstruck) sound, on the other hand, is the expansion of the supreme resonance (*paranāda*) arising from the root of the voiceless; it is conventionally established from the middle of the spinal column (*tantrī*) up to the cavity of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*), being designated by the sound of the central channel (*madhyamā-svara*). And the *anāhata-hata* (unstruck-struck) is that which unfolds based on both [the unstruck and struck], having its manifestation burst forth from the hearing-organ (*śaṣkulī*) where the struck sound comes to rest; it exists within the space situated between the two ears, arising from the body of reality (*tattva-deha*) as the reflection of reality (*tattva-pratibimba*).
It is both struck and unstruck, transcending even the unstruck;

it is the manifestation of the great abode free from obscuration, non-conceptual, and the primordial limit of the Great Vibration whose nature is slight movement. Being devoid of contraction and expansion, it is the form of supreme expansion, characterized by intangibility, and consists of the manifestation of the great mantra that cannot be uttered.
Likewise, that which transcends both the unstruck (*anāhata*) and the struck (*hata*) is the fourth state (*turya*), which has the form of a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (triangular) and is of the nature of Raudrī.

That which is both unstruck and struck has the configuration of a face consisting of the energy of the vowel-less (*anacka-kalā*) and is of the nature of Vāmā; this is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
And the unstruck is the power Ambikā, who is of the form of the arm as described in the *Yāga*; its essential nature is the state of dreaming (*svapna*).

"Slain," "the form of the weapon," "the nature of the eldest," and "awake"—this description of the fourfold nature of the first letter is a specific method of transmission through the lineage. Its power (*bala*) is the vitality (*vīrya*) consisting of the radiance of the sound that transcends the slain (*hata*), which flashes forth from the three forms beginning with the slain (*hata*) as the unstruck (*anāhata*). By means of that "power of the discourse on the ineffable."

In this regard, such non-speaking is the transcendence of verbal proliferation; indeed, non-speaking itself is speaking. Through the process of transition, it is the realization of the nature of the homeless state, which is precisely that power—the uncreated, expansive essence.
By means of that, the transition is here briefly elaborated.

The excellent teacher, having established his seat in the abode of consciousness— which is blossoming wavelessly— through the dissolution of the conceit that identifies with the limited subjects consisting of the vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void; and by the power of the vision of the supreme void,

which is beautiful with the bliss of motionlessness, perceives whatever he beholds, independent of the body, the senses, and karma, as being nothing other than the supreme, consisting of consciousness, through the realization of the nature of the all-pervading Self.
This is always so;
there is no doubt in this matter.

Furthermore, he states another interpretation: first, the teaching manifests through the support of the circles (*cakra*) of both fixed and unfixed deities as proclaimed in the sequence of worship within the collections of the *Ṣaḍdarśana*, the *Caturāmnāya*, and the *Melāpakrama*.

In this context, however, by abandoning the relationship between the worshiper, the object of worship, and the act of worship, and according to the oral tradition (*vaktrāmnāya*) of the preeminent perfected ones (*siddha*) such as the illustrious Vātūlanātha, [the Self] shines everywhere at all times, inseparable from its own nature which transcends all, like the constant expansion of the great rays of light that are eternally established;
such is the power of the discourse on the "inexpressible" (*akathanakathā*).
The connection is that one attains "great wonder" (*mahāvismaya*).

"Great wonder" is the departure—that is, the destruction—of *smaya*, which is the pride and arrogance of limited and unlimited ego; it is the entry into one's own true nature by way of transcending everything.
Furthermore, great wonder is the sudden immersion in the unimpeded, continuous state of the sky-farer (*khecara*), resulting from the forgetting of the distinction between self and other.
Because she embraces all mudrās, she is indeed the "mudrā"; her nature consists of immersion in the state of silence (*maunapada*).

By means of her as the cause, there arises the state of being "Khasvara"—the essence of Khasvara, which consists of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) in the narration of the thirteen stories; the meaning is that there occurs the manifestation of that aesthetic identity.
As for Khasvara: although "space" (*kha*) is devoid of existence, it "gives" (*rāti*), i.e., pervades, takes possession of, and assumes [all things] by its own nature.
Thus [ends] Khasvara.

Through the method of instruction on the direct realization of the thirteen discourses—the discourse on the assembly of all [teachings] belonging to the six philosophical systems and the four traditions—by virtue of the non-duality of the unsurpassed state, the oral tradition (vaktrāmnāya) bound in aphorisms was revealed by certain *avadhūtas* together with the *pīṭheśvarīs* at the time of the Great Assembly (*mahāmelāpa*). For the sake of the awakening of the wise, we have composed this commentary upon it; may there be auspiciousness!
Thus has this supreme secret, the flood of verbal conceptualization,

been correctly spoken by someone through the expansion of consciousness— an incomparable and lofty work composed by one liberated from the delusion of the distinction between existence and non-existence.
By means of a state of exultant activity that disregards the courage of other beings.
This commentary on the Śrīmad-Vātūlanātha-sūtra is completed. It is the work of the venerable Anantaśaktipāda.
By the command of the illustrious King Pratāpa, for the delight of the virtuous,
this work has been brought to completion and published by Madhusūdana Kaula.
